Julius Caesar. A Roman military commander, statesman, and author whose conquest of Gaul and subsequent civil war fundamentally transformed the Roman Republic into a de facto autocracy, establishing the template for imperial rule that would dominate the Mediterranean for centuries.

Caesar rose to prominence through military service in Spain and the Lusitanian Wars, then advanced through political offices including quaestor, aedile, and praetor, each campaign funded partly by his own wealth to win popular support. In 60 BCE, he formed the First Triumvirate with Pompeius and Crassus, a secret pact that united Rome's three most powerful men to dominate the city's politics. He served as consul in 59 BCE, using his office to pass laws favoring the triumvirs and securing for himself the lucrative province of Gaul for a five-year command.

From 58 to 50 BCE, Caesar launched a nine-year campaign to conquer Gaul, expanding Roman territory dramatically. His vivid account survives in the Commentarii de Bello Gallico, one of antiquity's most important historical texts. He defeated the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BCE, a siege-battle that broke the back of Gallic resistance and became the model for Roman siege warfare. Caesar crossed the Rhine to campaign against Germanic tribes and invaded Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE, conducting military operations in territories no Roman had previously conquered.

He accumulated immense wealth, military glory, and the loyalty of his legions, a power base that alarmed the Senate. When the Senate demanded he disband his army, Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, a river forming the border of Italy, with his legion, an act of military invasion that triggered civil war. The phrase "the die is cast" commemorates this decision to violate Roman law. He defeated Pompeius at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, the decisive battle of the civil war, then pursued Pompeius to Egypt where he allied with Cleopatra the seventh and defeated remaining Pompeian forces across the Mediterranean.

Caesar consolidated power as dictator for life, initiating sweeping reforms: he reformed the calendar, creating the Julian calendar that is the basis of our modern system; expanded citizenship; conducted land redistribution; and planned a campaign against Parthia, Rome's great eastern rival. On the Ides of March, March 15th, in 44 BCE, he was assassinated by a conspiracy of senators, including his protégé Brutus, who feared his autocratic rule and dreamed of restoring the Republic.

His will named his grandnephew Octavian, later Augustus, as his chief heir, effectively passing his political legacy to the man who would found the Roman Empire. His death triggered a second civil war and a cascade of events that destroyed the Republic and established the imperial autocracy that replaced it.
